newsitem.title: GERMANY: German banks brace for invasion of Thyssen workers.
newsitem.headline: German banks brace for invasion of Thyssen workers.

text.p: Germany's financial capital Frankfurt is bracing for an invasion on Tuesday of 30,000 steel workers of Thyssen AG intent on venting their wrath at the role of banks in a possible tie-up with Krupp AG.

The workers, who fear at least 7,000 jobs could be lost at the two companies, look set to paralyse traffic in Frankfurt by marching to the banking district. They will stage a rally a stone's throw from the twin-towered headquarters of Deutsche Bank AG.
Krupp, the full name of which is Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp, originally launched a hostile bid for Thyssen but later agreed to talks with its target on an agreed merger.
It set a Thursday deadline but Krupp already said on Tuesday its takeover bid was void and would not be renewed.
The two companies said in a joint statement that they were exploring cooperation which went beyond a merger of steel activities.
Whatever tie up may emerge, jobs are likely to be lost as the German steel industry tries to become more competitive.
The rally is being organised by engineering union IG Metall and will take place at midday. IG Metall's combative president Klaus Zwickel will be among the speakers.

Before the companies announced the hostile bid was off, several hundred Thyssen workers demonstrated outside a Deutsche Bank branch in Duesseldorf on Monday waving banners reading "Banks: Hands off Thyssen" and "Tell the bankers to shut up".
Deutsche Bank, Dresdner Bank AG and U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs advised Krupp in its bid for Thyssen.

They have been accused by politicians and union leaders of joining a corporate raid that goes against the grain of Germany's consensus culture and which could cause heavy job losses at a time of record post-war unemployment.

The affair has led to renewed calls for curbs on the power wielded by German banks through their large industrial shareholdings and the representation of bankers on many different company supervisory boards.

Krupp launched the bid last Tuesday but decided after intervention from politicians from all sides and resistance by steelworkers to shelve the takeover pending the talks on a possible uncontested merger.
In the joint statement, the companies said: "The negotiations between Thyssen and Krupp over a merger of steel operations are going well.
"The participants agree that such a merger would enable Germany to survive as a steel production centre and make possible a strategy to move forward."
Deutsche has borne the brunt of criticism because its management board member Ulrich Cartellieri is represented on Thyssen's supervisory board. He did not inform it of Krupp's impending bid.

But Deutsche on Monday hit back against criticism that it had engaged in "Wild West" tactics. "Talk by some politicians and trade unionists of conspiracy theories, Wild West manners, and claims to power by banks, lacks any foundation," it said in a statement.
Police said they did not expect any violence at the protest but would set up a security cordon outside the Deutsche Bank building to prevent workers gaining entry.
